title: Coalition support in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies
text:
Support across groups
Each dot is one party on one roll call. Most results sit at or near 100%, so the comparison rests on the average and on how often a party fell below 90%.

  
    
      Compare by
      
    
  
  
    Average
    Middle half of results, line at the median
    Party result on one roll call
  
  
  “Below 90%” is the share of party results in which fewer than 90% of the party's voting deputies followed the president. Party results with fewer than five deputies voting are left out. Dots and averages are not weighted by party size; the pooled column in the table counts every deputy vote equally. Centrão follows the classification in the replication data. Election timing follows the article's indicator for roll calls held after the first round of national or local elections.

title: Coalition support in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies
text:
Parties compared
Parties stay in the same order, from highest to lowest support for the president, so switching the measure shows how shares of posts and ideological distance line up with support.

  
    
      Show
      
    
  
  
    Centrão party
    Other party
    Range of coalition-year averages (3+ roll calls)
  
  
    
    
  
  Support is the share of the party's coalition votes that followed the president, with the range of its coalition-year averages over periods with at least three roll calls. Shares of posts are means of the party's year totals across the years it voted as a coalition member, with the lowest and highest year. Distance to the president's party is the article's ideological distance measure, averaged across the party's roll calls, with the range across years.

  These are simple correlations across party-years (2016 is split by president), without the party fixed effects and controls used in the article's models, so they can differ from the article's estimates. Variables keep the order of their correlation with support across all party-years, whatever the selection. “Within parties” subtracts each party's own average first, so only changes within parties over time remain; centrão does not vary within parties and drops out. Party-years with fewer than five votes are left out.

title: Coalition support in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies
text:
About the data
Every number on this page is computed from the article’s replication data and published only as party and coalition totals. Roll calls come from CEBRAP and appointments from ENAP. The charts are descriptive: they show associations in the data, without the controls used in the article’s models.

title: Koichi Osamura
text:
Political Scientist · Research Fellow at the University of Vienna


I study coalition politics, legislative behavior, and party competition, focusing on presidential systems in Latin America and parliamentary democracies in Western Europe.

I am a research fellow at the Department of Government, University of Vienna, where I obtained my doctorate in Political Science. Besides my substantive work, I enjoy learning new methods and techniques, especially new visualization tools.

title: Research
text:
Party Politics · 2026 · OnlineFirst
Bureaucratic appointments and coalition support in presidential systems: An analysis of Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies
Osamura, K.


Summary

Presidents in multiparty systems keep coalition partners on board not only with ministries but also with lower-level posts in the bureaucracy. Using roll-call votes on 161 bills in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies (2003–2018), I show that these appointments strongly increase legislative support for the government’s bills.

title: Research
text:
Dissertation


Seeking Office, Policy, or Votes? An Analysis of Legislative Coalitions, Motivations, and Behavior in Multiparty Presidential Systems

Supervision: Prof. Thomas M. Meyer, PhD, and Prof. Dr. Laurenz Ennser-Jedenastik
Committee: Chair: Prof. Markus Wagner (Vienna); External examiners: Prof. Timothy J. Power (Oxford), Assoc. Prof. Thiago Nascimento da Silva (Australian National University)


Summary

Most research on coalitions in presidential systems focuses on the president who builds them. My dissertation looks instead at the parties that join, stay in, or leave these governments, and at what they seek: office, policy, or votes. Three papers take each goal in turn, studying political appointments in Brazil, ideological distance and law-making in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, and the electoral fate of legislators who break with their party in Brazil and Chile.
